body: Being on your own can feel awkward, even uneasy. Over roughly ninety days, these notes will help you discover that your own company can be a place of rest.
Today, just notice the moments you are alone and what you instinctively reach for to fill them. No need to change anything.
Discomfort with being alone is very common. Many of us grew up with constant noise, company and screens, and silence feels unfamiliar.
Notice the difference between being alone and feeling lonely. They can overlap, but they are not the same thing.
If an empty evening makes you a little restless, that is not a sign something is wrong with you. It is simply a habit meeting quiet.
Pay attention to how quickly you pick up your phone when you are on your own. Count it today, without scolding yourself.
Some people learned early that being alone meant being left out. It makes sense if solitude still carries a faint sting.
You are the one person you will spend every single day with. It is worth getting to know them kindly.
Notice which kinds of quiet feel easier: a walk, a bath, a long drive. Those are good places to start.
Solitude does not have to be long to count. A few uninterrupted minutes on your own still matters.
If your thoughts get louder when the room goes quiet, that is normal. They often settle once they realise you are listening.
Think of someone who seems comfortable in their own company. What do you imagine they do with their time alone?
There is nothing selfish about wanting time to yourself, and nothing sad about enjoying it.
Notice how you speak to yourself when no one else is around. Would you say those things to a friend?
Two weeks in. Simply paying attention to how you feel when alone is already a quiet shift.
Today, sit with a cup of tea or coffee for five minutes without your phone, a book or the radio. Just the drink and the view.
Take a short walk alone with no headphones. Notice the sounds you usually miss.
Eat one meal on your own this week without a screen. Taste it properly. It may feel odd at first, and that is fine.
Look out of a window for three minutes. Watch the weather, the light, the passers-by. Let your mind wander where it likes.
Try leaving the television or podcast off for the first half hour after you get home. Notice what the silence feels like.
Restlessness in solitude often fades after the first ten minutes. See if you can stay through that awkward start.
Write a few lines in a notebook about your day, just for you. No one else needs to read it.
Take yourself somewhere small on your own: a bench, a gallery, a cafe. Treat it like meeting a friend.
Notice what you genuinely enjoy when no one else's preferences are in the room. Your tastes may surprise you.
Do something slowly today that you usually rush: washing up, folding laundry, making a sandwich. Let it be the whole activity.
If you feel the urge to message someone just to fill a gap, pause for a minute first. You can still send it afterwards.
Spend ten minutes doing absolutely nothing. Sit, breathe, look around. Boredom is often the doorway to rest.
Plan a small solo treat for the weekend: a film, a bakery, a swim. Something you would happily do with a friend.
Four weeks along. Think of one moment alone recently that felt a little easier, or even pleasant.
Try a different kind of solitude this week: early morning, late evening, outdoors, or in a busy place where no one knows you.
Notice which thoughts tend to show up when you are alone. Some may be worries; some may be ideas worth keeping.
Listen to a whole album on your own, start to finish, without doing anything else. Let the music be enough.
Cook something just for yourself with the same care you would give a guest.
Go to bed a little earlier one night and read in the quiet. Notice how the end of the day feels without noise.
Notice the small pleasures that only happen when you are alone: singing badly, dancing in the kitchen, choosing the music.
If you live with others, find a pocket of solitude anyway: a walk round the block, a quiet bath, ten minutes in the car.
Try a solo outing a bit further afield: a day trip, a museum, a long walk somewhere new. Let yourself set the pace.
If being alone brings up sadness one day, let it be there. Feelings tend to move through when you stop pushing them away.
Notice how much energy you spend performing for others. Solitude is a place where you can put that down.
Practise listening to your own preferences. Where would you like to walk? What would you like to eat? Answer just for you.
Spend some time with something living: tending a plant, watching birds, sitting under a tree. Solitude need not feel empty.
Sit in a cafe or park on your own and resist the urge to look busy. You are allowed simply to be there.
Halfway through. Notice whether your evenings alone feel different from how they felt at the start.
Try writing yourself a short letter about what you hope your time alone can become.
Take a photograph of something beautiful you found while alone today. It is a small record of good company.
Notice whether you are kinder or harsher with yourself in the quiet. Gently tilt the balance towards kindness.
Give yourself one unscheduled hour this week. No plan, no list. See what you naturally drift towards.
Learn something small purely for your own interest: a bird call, a constellation, a recipe, a word in another language.
If you catch yourself filling every silence with noise, try lowering the volume rather than switching it off. Small steps count.
Watch the sunset or sunrise on your own. Let it take as long as it takes.
Solitude and connection are partners, not rivals. Time alone often makes time with others feel richer.
Notice what you think about when your mind is truly free. That wandering is where a lot of self-knowledge lives.
Try a quiet hobby that rewards patience: a jigsaw, a sketch, a crossword, a slow-cooked meal.
Turn off notifications for an afternoon and spend it on your own terms. Notice the spaciousness that appears.
Be curious about the version of you that shows up alone. Is it calmer, sillier, more thoughtful? All of it belongs.
If plans fall through and you end up with an empty evening, try treating it as a gift rather than a disappointment.
Eight weeks in. Moments alone that once felt like waiting may now feel more like living.
You are becoming someone who can sit with themselves without needing to be rescued from the quiet.
You are becoming someone who chooses time alone on purpose, not just someone who puts up with it.
Some days solitude will still feel uncomfortable. That does not cancel out the good days; it simply sits alongside them.
Notice that you can now spend time alone without explaining or apologising for it, at least sometimes.
Plan a longer stretch of solitude: a slow morning, a whole afternoon, even a night away if that appeals. Shape it gently.
When someone asks what you did at the weekend, try saying you enjoyed some time to yourself. Notice how it feels to say it plainly.
If a hard week leaves you avoiding the quiet again, be patient. Habits loosen and tighten; you can return to stillness any time.
Finding rest in your own company is a skill you have been practising. Skills get steadier with use.
Notice the difference between solitude that restores you and isolation that drains you. You get to choose more of the first.
Make a short list of your favourite solo activities from these weeks. It is a menu you can return to whenever you like.
If others find it strange that you enjoy being alone, you do not need to convince them. Your rest is yours.
Take your notebook somewhere quiet and write about who you are when no one is watching. Be generous with yourself.
Ten weeks along. The silence that once felt like a gap may now have room in it for you.
You are becoming someone who knows how to keep themselves good company on an ordinary Tuesday evening.
Let solitude be a place where you notice what you need: more sleep, more air, more people, less noise. Then act kindly on it.
A setback might be a lonely evening that hits harder than expected. Be gentle, reach out if you want to, and know it will pass.
Try a small solo adventure this week, something you would once have only done with company. Notice how capable you are.
Notice how your thinking clears after time on your own. Decisions often feel simpler after a bit of quiet.
Being comfortable alone makes it easier to choose company because you want it, not because you dread the alternative.
Spend a few minutes before sleep noticing one thing you enjoyed about your own company today.
Your inner world is worth spending time in. It holds memories, ideas, opinions and dreams that are entirely yours.
Eleven weeks in. Recall one stretch of time alone recently that felt full rather than empty.
If old discomfort comes back in future, you now know some ways in: a walk, a quiet cup of tea, a notebook, a window.
Look back at how you felt about being alone at the start. Notice what has softened, even slightly.
You do not have to love every minute alone. Enjoying more of it than you used to is a genuine change.
Choose one small solo ritual to keep: a Sunday walk, a quiet breakfast, ten silent minutes in the evening.
Twelve weeks ago, quiet may have felt like something to escape. Notice how it feels to you today.
Think about how you would like solitude to fit into your life over the coming months. A loose rhythm is plenty.
Write down three things you have learned about yourself in the quiet. Keep them as a reminder of who you are.
Some seasons will be busy and full of people, others quieter. You can be at home in yourself through both.
Protect a little regular time alone going forward. It is maintenance, not indulgence.
The person who once felt uneasy in an empty room was doing their best. Offer them some warmth for getting you here.
Spend a little time alone today simply enjoying it, as a quiet thank you to yourself for these weeks.
Your own company has become somewhere you can rest. Carry that steadiness with you into busier days.
This is the final note in this series. May you keep finding rest, curiosity and warmth in the time you spend with yourself.
